title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) and model_calls_used = 200. Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, give an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and provide concrete, archive‑supported design recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the exploratory reserve, and pilot contingency checks) required for informative repeats.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate human intent into network device configuration changes to accelerate NetOps tasks and reduce operator load. However, erroneous or improperly ordered changes can cause outages, break reachability, or violate security policies. A common mitigation strategy is tool‑augmentation: couple an LLM generator with deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors so that proposed changes are checked before execution.

Motivated by this operational risk, we preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to test whether adding a deterministic sandbox validator to an LLM pipeline causally reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals. Our primary estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across N=200 intent→configuration tasks, analyzed with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm draws (one model call per arm per task) or shared_initial_candidate (a single shared LLM candidate per task scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve hosted model budget.

Key empirical outcome: under the executed shared semantics every confirmatory candidate was labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator in both arms (baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200), producing a degenerate contingency (n11=200, n10=n01=n00=0), an estimated paired difference of 0.0, p = 1.0, and a degenerate 95% CI [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline unsafe rate was zero and both arms scored the same candidate, the preregistered causal contrast was not testable. The remainder of the paper (1) documents the reproducible, preregistered run; (2) provides an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the execution was non‑informative for the intended estimand; and (3) gives concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations to make repeats informative while preserving preregistration rigor.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototypes document rapid adoption of LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited remediation) while warning about safety and evaluation gaps (e.g., workflow‑centred, replayable validation) observed across recent literature [Bilal et al., 2026; Ferrag et al., 2026; Fan Liu et al., 2024]. A recurring technical pattern is tool‑augmentation: pairing LLM generation with deterministic validators or simulators (generate–validate–refine and divide–verify–refine pipelines) to reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks [Divide‑Verify‑Refine, 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Empirical studies in adjacent domains show that verifier‑in‑the‑loop designs can improve measured adherence to constraints but that gains depend heavily on verifier fidelity, sampling semantics, and whether repairs are permitted and instrumented [VeriQuant, 2026; Okula, 2026].

Work on guardrails, schema interfaces, and agent orchestration emphasizes trade‑offs: stricter deterministic checks can lower the acceptance of unsafe proposals but may raise false‑refusal rates and operator burden if validators are incomplete or overconservative [Ando, 2026; Okula, 2026]. These studies motivate ROC‑style diagnostics for verifier behavior and call for exploratory reserves to quantify true‑positive/false‑positive trade‑offs in adversarial settings. Our experiment adopts the workflow‑centred, sandboxed evaluation ethos advocated in this literature: deterministic task generation, archived validator traces, and preregistered estimands and analysis plans so that runs are reproducible and interpretable under clearly stated semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) where each arm’s binary outcome is derived from deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test; CI: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified N=200 paired tasks, exclusions, retry rules, exploratory reserves (up to 50 tasks) for ROC estimation, and two permitted generation semantics.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic task generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration items (single‑AS, multi‑device topologies) constrained to fields {admin, mtu, vlan}. Each task manifest included initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit workflow policies (required_sequence), and difficulty metadata. Tasks were clustered into benign and adversarial transforms under a preregistered obfuscation rule set intended to increase adversarial difficulty; these rules were part of the preregistration.

Pipelines compared. Baseline pipeline: accept the LLM candidate (no runtime gate) and evaluate post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded pipeline: validate the (same or repaired) candidate in a deterministic sandbox using deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repair calls were permitted by the preregistration but, for confirmatory episodes, no repairs were applied in the archived run (repair traces are null).

Generation semantics and budget. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per task ⇒ planned model_calls up to 400) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task ⇒ 200 calls). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate for budget reasons; model_calls_used = 200 (execution manifest). This choice meant arms scored identical initial candidates unless the guarded arm applied a deterministic repair (which it did not in this run).

Scoring and analysis. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministic full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted structured traces (validation_before/after, violation lists). Confirmatory binary labels were validator.valid. The paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor computed contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. Missingness and contamination rules were applied deterministically: one automatic retry per failed model call; contaminated or nondeterministic tasks would be excluded and replaced (no such exclusions occurred). All raw inputs, responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied bundle for deterministic replay.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The archived execution_manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider audit confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and no call failures. Deterministic reconciliation checks passed and no exclusions or nondeterminism were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The resulting contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. From these counts: paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These values are direct outputs of paired_binary_analysis_v1 and are archived.

Representative diagnostic traces. Representative scoring JSONs show identical shared_initial_candidate content used by both arms and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true. Repair_provider_trace fields are null across confirmatory episodes, confirming that no automatic repairs were invoked and that the guarded arm performed validation only. The absence of repairs and the shared candidate semantics mechanically precluded discordant pair outcomes originating from arm‑level generation stochasticity.

Missingness and exploratory reserves. The analysis missingness summary documents complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes; contamination summary contains no flags. The preregistration’s exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks for ROC/refusal diagnostics) was not consumed prior to the confirmatory run, so no ROC data appear in the confirmatory artifacts.

Statistical interpretation. McNemar’s test relies on discordant pairs (n10 and n01) to detect a paired difference. The observed ceiling contingency (all concordant SAFE pairs) renders the preregistered inferential machinery non‑informative for the causal estimand: the test produces p = 1.0 and a degenerate CI, not evidence of verifier effectiveness. The archived run therefore demonstrates a testability failure driven by the conjunction of shared generation semantics, a zero observed baseline unsafe rate for the sampled model under the given adversarial transforms, and the absence of repairs that could have produced arm‑level divergence.
sections.discussion:
Root cause synthesis. The archive shows three deterministic facts that explain the non‑informative result: (1) execution used shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task) so both arms scored the same candidate; (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every candidate as valid (baseline SAFE = 200/200); (3) no repairs were applied, so the guarded arm did not alter candidates. Together these facts mechanically prevented discordance and thus invalidated the preregistered power assumptions (which had assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%).

Implications for confirmatory design. A paired estimand that attributes a causal effect to adding a validator requires per‑arm opportunities for divergence. Under shared semantics, discordance can only arise from repairs in the guarded arm or from nondeterministic validator behavior. To make the estimand testable while preserving paired analysis, experimenters should:
- Allocate budget for independent per‑arm generation in confirmatory runs (≈400 model calls for N=200) when repairs are not expected to induce discordance; the execution manifest quantifies that independent draws cost ~200 extra calls compared with the executed shared run.
- Consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate matches power assumptions; archive tuning runs and freeze transform parameters before confirmatory execution.
- Instrument and archive repair_provider_trace artifacts when repairs are enabled, and quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any secondary violations introduced by repairs.
- Run a deterministic pilot (small holdout) to detect ceiling/floor contingencies before committing to the full confirmatory test; if the pilot yields no discordance, apply preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptations (e.g., switch to independent per‑arm draws or strengthen adversarial injections) rather than proceeding with an uninformative confirmatory test.

Alternative estimands. When independent per‑arm draws are infeasible, alternative estimands remain testable under shared semantics: (a) estimate the LLM baseline absolute unsafe‑proposal rate with CIs; (b) treat the validator as an accept/reject gate and estimate refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates (requires repairs); or (c) use the exploratory reserve to estimate verifier ROC characteristics by injecting ground‑truth unsafe examples. These alternatives were listed in the preregistration and map directly to archived secondary_estimands and exploratory items.

Threats to validity and generalization. The synthetic task family restricted fields and topology scope; the deterministic validator encodes the full_intent_constraint_validation for that family but is not validated against production‑scale, multi‑vendor failure modes. Thus zero unsafe detections here do not imply production safety. External validity is limited by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini only) and by the particular adversarial transforms used; stronger adversarial injections or multi‑model evaluations are required for broader conclusions.

Operational implications. The run exposes a resource/estimand trade‑off operators face: conserving model calls via shared generation can make a paired causal contrast untestable; spending extra calls to allow independent per‑arm draws or consuming exploratory reserves yields informative diagnostics but costs resources. Our archived artifacts quantify these trade‑offs so teams can make informed budgeting decisions before repeating the experiment. Finally, because repairs were not invoked in the confirmatory episodes, we cannot estimate false‑refusal vs repair benefit trade‑offs here; future repetitions should instrument and analyze repair traces to measure that operational burden.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced verifier‑safe outputs on every confirmatory episode (baseline = 200/200 SAFE; guarded = 200/200 SAFE), yielding a degenerate contingency (n11=200) and non‑informative confirmatory inference (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). The primary scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the design failed to be informative under the executed semantics; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using exploratory reserves, pilot contingency checks, and repair instrumentation) required to produce informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts referenced here are archived in the supplied bundle for deterministic replay and audit; researchers attempting repeats should consult those artifacts and adopt the recommendations before re‑running confirmatory tests.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
